title: Trump’s ‘Diesel Deal’ With Russia Was Just the Start | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Sestanovich argues Trump's Russian diesel deal was the start of a sharper turn: calling for Zelenskyy's removal, inventing an energy-strike ceasefire, pressing Ukraine unilaterally and reportedly threatening intelligence and Starlink access, while Europe and Congress respond weakly.

insights.claim: Trump's deal to buy more Russian diesel by relaxing sanctions was likely illegal, made without consulting allies, and a near-certain violation of the 2022 Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sestanovich
entities: Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act
insights.so_what: Russian export earnings rise and legal and sanctions risk grows.
insights.locator: Sure, the decision to buy more diesel

insights.claim: A week after the deal, Trump called for Zelenskyy's removal and claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to suspend attacks on each other's energy targets, which was pure invention.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sestanovich
insights.so_what: Claims about energy-strike truces are unreliable; Russian refinery and Ukrainian grid targeting remains live.
insights.locator: A day after announcing new diesel imports

insights.claim: US negotiators reportedly pressed Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries unilaterally rather than via a mutual ceasefire, and Zelenskyy acceded for several days before saying we're done.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sestanovich
insights.so_what: Ukrainian refinery strikes, a driver of Russian fuel supply, may be curtailed or resumed on US pressure.
insights.locator: Reports suggested what had actually happened

insights.claim: Ukrainian and European officials reported US threats to cut intelligence sharing and weapons sales paid for by Europe, with reports of Starlink cuts hampering Ukrainian operations, following a pattern of denial followed by awkward acknowledgment.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sestanovich
insights.so_what: Watch Starlink availability and US-supplied intelligence as Ukraine's operational dependencies.
insights.locator: Ukrainian representatives who met last week

insights.claim: Trump now casts Zelenskyy as the single real obstacle to peace, and Sestanovich says he now seems to pursue a final settlement and pressure on Zelenskyy instead of partial de-escalation or Putin.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sestanovich
insights.so_what: If sustained, peace terms would tilt toward Russia.
insights.quote: Rather than work on partial de-escalation of the fighting

insights.claim: Ukraine's formula of public gratitude and behind-the-scenes lawyerly haggling has been nearly reversed, with Zelenskyy publicly criticizing US decisions but quietly complying in practice.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sestanovich
insights.so_what: Kyiv-Washington friction signals less US support.
insights.locator: It is hard to overstate how much this new public hostility

themes.theme: Weak response from Europe and Congress

insights.claim: European leaders show confusion and no unified pushback, unlike after the Alaska summit with Putin, and even NATO's Mark Rutte has said little, though the UK offered a military package under new PM Andy Burnham.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sestanovich
insights.so_what: European defense support may fill gaps but coordinated leverage on Washington is absent.
insights.locator: European leaders show the same confusion

insights.claim: Congressional response is muted, limited to a letter by six Democratic and six Republican senators and another by twenty-two House members, as midterms dominate attention.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sestanovich
insights.so_what: Low odds of congressional constraint on sanctions relief.

insights.claim: Many assume Trump will back off as before, but Sestanovich warns that if his changed view persists, a dangerous period of prolonged Ukrainian suffering, lasting damage to US alliances and bitter domestic debate lies ahead.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sestanovich
insights.so_what: Do not assume a reversal; plan for sustained US pressure on Kyiv.
